claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloy superconductors is predominantly governed by the electronic density of states at the Fermi level rather than atomic-scale disorder.
The effective valence electron count modulates the density of states at the Fermi level.
Reducing atomic-scale disorder through annealing will not significantly change the superconducting transition temperature.
Reducing atomic-scale disorder through annealing will not significantly change the superconducting coherence length.
The target as-cast alloys are equiatomic, single-phase disordered solid solutions in the dirty limit.
Post-synthesis annealing can reduce atomic-scale disorder while preserving overall composition and phase stability.
The comparison is restricted to samples that remain in the dirty limit after annealing.
The density of states at the Fermi level is primarily set by overall valence electron count rather than variations in atomic-scale disorder.
In the studied (TaNb)1-x(ZrHfTi)x films, the observed composition-dependent transition-temperature variation cannot be explained by disorder effects.
Electronic doping can change the density of states at the Fermi level and thereby account for transition-temperature variations within a classical BCS framework.
Annealing may sharpen local structural features while leaving the density of states at the Fermi level largely unchanged.
An annealing-invariant density of states will leave electron-phonon coupling nearly unchanged.
Annealed and as-cast samples will have similar tunneling spectra.
The proposed conclusion applies only when annealing does not cause compositional segregation or phase separation.
The proposed conclusion is limited to high-entropy alloy superconductors with transition temperatures of approximately 2–10 K.
Known high-entropy alloy superconductors can exhibit conventional BCS superconductivity with intermediate-to-strong coupling.
Local ordering induced by annealing could cause minor changes in superconducting characteristics, but these effects would be secondary to electron-count effects.
